terms.definition: Our multi-model system. Three specialist models each answer part of a question, and an editor model combines their answers into one report.

One of the models on the council, each given one field: healthcare, legal or finance. The first council used Med42 (healthcare), Saul (legal) and Qwen-Open-Finance (finance). Many later cells used a general model given the specialist's role in its prompt.
The model that plans the work, reads the specialists' drafts and writes the final answer. Phi-4 14B held this job at first, and gpt-oss-20B for most of the later work.
The editor's first job: splitting the question into parts and deciding which specialists to ask.
One of the 18 business-advisory questions every setup answered, such as rolling out an AI sepsis-warning tool across 12 hospitals.
A simple scenario that calls for no caveats at all. It catches models that hedge everywhere instead of only where it is warranted.
One experiment. Cells are numbered in the order they were planned, with letters for close relatives (6b, 6c) and "-R" for a repeat (43-R). Cell IV is a Roman numeral: a check of a measuring method.
One way of running an experiment, compared against another way. For example, the editor with an extra instruction and the editor without it.
One complete pass of a setup on one scenario, from the question to the final answer. Most cells repeat each run several times because models give different answers each time.

A published recipe for combining models: several general-purpose models answer, then one model merges their answers. We used it as a second design to check whether our findings were specific to our council.

The redesigned council, built only from parts that held up in testing and tested piece by piece from Cell 47 onward. It gives key numbers to two specialists on purpose, carries caveats in a separate section, and sends follow-up questions back to specialists. In early August the lab notes also use "harness" for an earlier package of measuring and checking tools, which is a different thing.

A sentence that flags uncertainty or a limit, such as "this figure is an estimate" or "the rules differ in Germany". Whether caveats survive from the specialists into the final answer was the project's first big question.

also: families: cutoff, modeled, precise, jurisdictional, hedging
terms.definition: The categories we counted: my information may be out of date, this number is an estimate, these two terms mean different things, the rules differ by place, and general hedging.
How much cautious language a text contains, counted per 1,000 characters. The early cells report it for the specialists' drafts and for the final answer.

The formula for how caveats move from the specialists into the final answer. Here s is how much caution the specialists handed over and y is how much reaches the final answer. The early cells count kinds of caveat, and the later cells scored by AI judges (Cell 30 onward) count sentences that carry a caveat. The share passed along is w, and c is how much the editor adds on its own when handed none.

terms.term: Caution the editor adds on its own
terms.definition: Caveats that appear in the final answer even though no specialist raised them. Cell 38 found this happens even when the drafts contain no caveats at all.
The amount of caution a given editor model tends to produce whatever its input. Early cells found each editor has its own.
A passage in the editor's prompt telling it to keep the specialists' caveats. Cells 6, 13 and 14 tested what it does.
Exact phrases our prompts told models to use, such as "modeled at". Counting those phrases measures obedience, not caution, which PD-13 and Cell 41 showed directly.
Further training of an existing model on new examples to specialize it. The first council's specialists were fine-tuned versions of general models.
Fine-tuning by showing a model good example answers to imitate. Cell 1 compared it with preference training.
Fine-tuning by showing a model pairs of answers, one preferred and one rejected, so it learns to favor the better kind. ORPO, CPO and DPO are three versions.
Three preference-training methods. The project trained with ORPO and CPO. A bug in the training software ruled out DPO itself, although some run names still say "dpo".
A reward-based training method: the model writes several answers and is pushed toward the ones that score best. Cell 16 planned to use it and could not run it on our hardware.
A lightweight way to fine-tune. A small add-on is trained instead of the whole model, which let us train on one machine.
A base model is trained only to continue text. An instruct model has been further trained to follow instructions and hold a conversation.
A model that writes hidden working notes before it answers. gpt-oss-20B and Qwen3 work this way, so a length limit set too low can leave them with no room for the answer itself.
The unit AI models read and write in, roughly three quarters of an English word. Length limits are set in tokens.
Standing instructions given to a model before the question itself.
A setting for how much randomness a model uses when choosing words. At temperature 0 it always picks its most likely next word.
Before each cell ran, we wrote down what we expected, what result would prove us wrong, and what we would do either way. The plans were saved in version control before the first run.
One specific result we expected before a cell ran. Each has an id such as P25.1 (Cell 25, expectation 1) so it can be traced in the lab notes.
An adjustment to a cell's plan, written down before any of its results were seen.
A stopping rule set in advance. If a pilot run failed it, the experiment stopped instead of carrying on.
A separate model asked to compare or grade answers. Many cells used judges from two different model families, so one family's quirks could not decide a result alone.
An AI judge's habit of preferring whichever answer it reads first. Our judges picked the first answer 85% to 88% of the time, so every comparison was shown in both orders.
A comparison where the judge picked the same answer in both orders. Everything else counts as a tie.

A scoring method that counts words and phrases from a fixed list. From 9 August 2026 the project stopped using it as a measuring tool, because prompts had told models to use the very phrases it counted.
A model that judges whether one sentence follows from another. Cells 7a and 23 tried it as a caveat detector.

Two AI judges labeling each sentence of an answer separately. It became the project's main measuring tool after Cell 23, and Cell IV checked that judging sentences in batches of 10 keeps its accuracy.
The range the true value could reasonably fall in, given how few runs there were. When the range for a head-to-head test includes 50%, the result is too close to call.
The data could not separate the possibilities, usually because too few runs gave a clear answer.
A question the system sends back to a specialist when the drafts disagree, so the editor gets the deciding fact.
A list the editor must write of the points where the specialists' drafts conflict, before it writes the answer. Software reads it to decide which follow-ups to send.
A section attached to the end of the final report that carries the specialists' caveats directly. The editor never rewrites it, so nothing is lost on the way.
Giving the same key number to two specialists on purpose, so one wrong draft cannot decide the answer on its own.
A check a model must pass before it can serve as a specialist. It has to produce real answers rather than garbled, repetitive or empty ones.

A filter that catches made-up legal citations the live specialists were found to repeat. It screens specialists' follow-up replies before the editor sees them and never feeds anything back to the specialist.
